speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: My response will also address related oral and written questions filed for the Sitting on 4 August 2026.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Candidates are first seated at the silent preparation station.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: The candidates view a computer screen with three components simultaneously displayed.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: The examination instructions, a text prompt and a video.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: They are given 10 minutes at this station to prepare a planned response to their oral presentation.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: After 10 minutes, the candidate is called to the examiners' station.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: The oral examiner reads out the same text prompt and invites the candidate to commence the presentation.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Candidates are given two minutes to deliver their planned response.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: This is followed by the spoken interaction component, where the candidate engages in a discussion with the oral examiners on a topic based on the video clip.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: All examination materials are subjected to a rigorous and secure process of authoring, review and approval.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: The oral examinations are accessed through the Singapore Examinations and Assessment Board's (SEAB's) e-Examination system.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Digital logs monitor all activities carried out in the system to ensure the integrity of the processes.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: For each oral examination session, only one version of the examination materials is stored on SEAB's e-Examination system.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: All examination centres access the same materials when they log into SEAB's e-Examination system.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: The materials are encrypted and can only be accessed by authorised personnel.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Before the start of each session, the Assessment Specialist at SEAB checks that the prompt shown on-screen to candidates during the silent preparation and the prompt shown to the oral examiners tally exactly with the prompt on the question paper in hard copy.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Once the examination has commenced, the materials cannot be amended.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: During the examination, all stations in the examination centres, including the candidates silent preparation stations and the oral examiners stations, access the same approved, secured, encrypted examination materials from the e-Examination system.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: There were 389 oral examination teams across schools, with each team comprising two trained oral examiners assessing 13 candidates per session.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: The video presented to candidates depicted street barbers at work.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: The prompt for the planned response segment was, "Who do you think would go to a place like this for a haircut?

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: On 15 July itself, SEAB took immediate actions to investigate.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: SEAB verified the examination materials by making system level checks and by logging into candidates' individual accounts in the e-Examination system, which shows the prompt and video accessed by the candidates.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: SEAB subsequently also reviewed all the digital logs of the authoring and delivery of the examination material from SEAB's e-Examination system and the digital logs of what was displayed on individual candidates' screens during the silent preparation, for all candidates who reported a discrepancy.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: In addition, cybersecurity checks were conducted to ascertain if the e-Examination system had been compromised.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Investigations showed that in all examination centres, oral examiners and candidates accessed the same examination materials during the oral examination on 15 July 2026.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: There was no evidence of a system malfunction.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: There was no discrepancy in the prompt displayed to candidates and oral examiners.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: There was only one source that all candidates' and examiners' accounts accessed.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We also observed no discernible pattern of these incidents.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: The 432 candidates who reported this discrepancy came from 200 different oral examiner teams.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: There was also no particular order to the affected candidate.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: For instance, it was the second and eighth out of 13 candidates for one oral exam team.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: So, in that sequence, this oral exam team would examine 13 candidates, and it was the second and eighth candidate reporting a discrepancy with the other candidates reporting no discrepancy.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: And for another oral team, it was the third and 10th candidate, for example.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: To be clear, the discrepancies reported were not about what the oral examiners asked – only that the recollection of the text prompt at the preparation station was different from what the oral examiner read out.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: The reported discrepancies also demonstrated significant variation, with different phrases recalled by different students, including by students that were examined at the same centre and by the same oral examination team.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: The actual prompt shown was, "Who do you think would go to a place like this for a haircut?

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Why do you say so?" Some candidates reported reading the prompt as, "Would you go?" Others reported reading the prompt as, "Would you visit?", "Would you be interested?", "Would you like?", "Would you want?", "Would you cut your hair at the place shown?", "Would you get your hair cut?" and "Why would I go?" Putting together the technical details, the distribution pattern of the incidents across the stations, schools and time, as well as the variety of phrases reported by the students.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We understand that the experience would have been unsettling for the affected candidates.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Parents and candidates can be assured that our oral examiners are experienced teachers who assessed candidates based on what they demonstrated during the examination, including how they developed and presented their ideas and opinions, and how effectively they engaged the examiner during the discussion.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: So, therefore, as a group, the candidates who reported discrepancies fared as well as other candidates who did not report any discrepancy.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: There might be some candidates who experienced significant distress arising from the circumstances.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: This might have affected their ability to provide a suitable response.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Schools are working with these candidates to apply for special consideration.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Special consideration is an established evidence-based process by examination boards to review the final subject grades for candidates whose performance had been adversely affected by circumstances beyond their control during the examinations.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Each application will be evaluated on its merits.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We thank candidates, parents and schools for bringing their concerns to our attention.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: SEAB conducted a thorough investigation before coming to the conclusion that the same prompt was displayed for all candidates.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: SEAB also remains committed to ensuring that all candidates, including those who might have misread the prompt, are assessed fairly.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: In relation to the special considerations that he shared with this House earlier, I also understand from my resident that that has been the reply from SEAB to one of my residents whose child has been affected.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: In this regard, can I enquire so far in relation to the over 500 cases that were reported of discrepancies that were highlighted – 400 plus in total, I beg your pardon – have any of these students followed up with a special consideration application?

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: The process of special consideration is still in process.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: So, I think it is perhaps not appropriate for me to comment on the specifics.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: The process of special consideration is to look at the particular circumstances of each case.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Certainly, some applications have been made and potentially further applications will be made.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: So, I think we have to let that process play out.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: First, if I may paraphrase what I am hearing as the explanation or what the investigation has uncovered, is that the system architecture by its very nature would not permit the incident that students are describing from happening – because of the nature of the fact that it is a single question stored in the database and it is a single question transmitted to all terminals.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: That being said, I understand also that centralised logs were also checked to make sure that this was indeed what happened.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Can the Ministry share if the terminals themselves maintained any logs and whether these logs can be investigated to see whether what was displayed or was it recorded what was actually displayed on the screen of the individual terminals, as opposed to the centralised database?

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: My second supplementary question is essentially on the nature of the question itself.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It would seem that given that the Ministry of Education (MOE) is convinced that no actual variation in the question displayed happened, but about 8% to 9% of students who took the exam experienced this, would MOE consider varying the way they set oral examination questions in the future?

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I understand that reading comprehension is one of the elements being tested in an oral examination, but I would argue it is probably not the main element being tested.

speaker: Mr Low Wu Yang Andre (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Would MOE consider in the future of setting questions or user testing questions such that such incidents would not arise again in the future and cause potential distress to our students?

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: On his first point, indeed, the investigation involved the individual terminals, including logging on with the student's ID and authentication, so that the exact same handshake between the terminal and the centralised database was carried out, to see what was returned as material.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: And part of that technical professional skillset is to look at how specific phrases or words are used within examination prompts.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I accept that SEAB did their due diligence in verifying that there were no computer issues that could have given rise to the alleged outcome, and it is on this basis that the Senior Minister of State has asserted that that there were no errors.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: I wonder then is SEAB implicitly suggesting that there could have been an occasion of collective hallucination that occurred on that day?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: And if so, does this mean that the investigation would have perhaps implicitly privileged computer forensic evidence over the contemporary testimony of a significant number of human witnesses?

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: And as our investigations have demonstrated, the students demonstrated significant variance in the many phrases that they recalled.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: So, I think his implication that we are privileging one set of information over the other is incorrect.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: We are looking at both the testimonies, as well as the technical assessment.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: And the fact that the testimonies covered a wide variation in the phrases in itself is a very significant data point.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: So, I would ask him to perhaps not put words in my mouth about collective hallucinations, nor imply a privileging of one set of data over the other.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: I think in my response, I have explained how we take all the data very seriously.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Reports were filed on that day by SEAB's own examination personnel at the schools.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: So, how many irregularity reports did SEAB receive concerning 15 July English oral exam?

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Not complaints from candidates, but actual reports filed by its own oral examiners and presiding officers.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: And if the Ministry does not have this figure today, will they undertake to provide it?

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: It seems very peculiar to me that 432 candidates from 132 schools reported it on day three, and day three alone.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: They did not report it on day one, day two or day four.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Supplementary question two: did SEAB examine the candidates' contemporaneous physical planning sheets against the examiner's script?

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: But the information from the contemporaneous planning sheets does, in some cases indicate that the student had misread the prompt.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: And in some cases, it indicates that the student had misread the prompt, started planning on that basis and then corrected themselves.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: And so on one sheet, we can see the student having written down what they thought originally what is the prompt, and then crossing that out and then writing the correct prompt and then planning from there.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: And they have come to the same conclusion as SEAB.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: My question comes from conversations with parents who accept the fact that their children might have misinterpreted or misread the question under examination pressure.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: First, is the ability to accurately process a question under exam pressure, part of a skill to be accessed under oral examination?

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Second, if so, how are students prepared for this, because, unlike written exams, which students experience across many subjects, they may have fewer opportunities to practise this skillset to respond under exam pressure.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Third, parents would like to know, when candidates reported the question has been asked differently from what they saw in the terminal, could we clarify what was the process thereafter?

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: His first two questions, I think, are a little bit outside the remit of this Parliamentary Question, which is about the examination process; and more about the overall preparation for the subject, the curriculum and the approach taken to prepare students.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: But across all subjects, certainly, the way in which our students approach an examination is very much part of the preparation in the classroom, in the development of the student across the curriculum, across the syllabus and the skills and techniques that they learn in the classroom.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: And some of that will be about how to deal with errors, deal with the emotional state that they are in.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: So, I think it is quite beyond the remit of the Parliamentary Question today, but I thank him for highlighting this.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: It is indeed an important part of the work that is done by the teachers.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: He then asked about the process after reporting.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Can I just ask what is it he was asking about?

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: I did not quite understand what he meant.

speaker: Mr David Hoe
text: Basically, parents are questioning, after a child report that the question that they saw on the terminal and the question asked was different, what happened after?

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Mr Hoe has clarified that he is talking about what is happening with the examiner rather than the investigation of the incident.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: They are not looking for absolute compliance with a template answer.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: They are looking in this exam, for the students to demonstrate their skill, their oral skill with their language – what vocabulary they are using, their sentence structure, how they use grammar and tense, how they present their ideas, how they organise their ideas and how they build upon ideas over the course of the presentation.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: And this is one of the reasons why you can see that the marks are comparable.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: Sometimes, they had prepared incorrectly, but nevertheless were able to speak well, either on the initial subject that they thought they were presenting on or when corrected on the prompt that they heard from the examiner.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: And so, within their presentation was enough material demonstrating their ability with the language.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: This approach of positive marking then allows the examiner to draw out the skills that the student has and provide them an appropriate mark.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: And it applies regardless of whether the students hesitate, perhaps, ask a question about the prompt.

speaker: Dr Janil Puthucheary
text: There is this approach of positive marking: looking for the ability of the student to demonstrate the skills that they have, not blind compliance with a template, nor a negative marking approach looking for mistakes.
